title: Symmetry-Aware Bayesian Optimization via Max Kernels
one_liner: When a real-world optimization problem has natural symmetries, a projected max kernel lets the optimizer exploit them to find good answers faster.
lead: Bayesian Optimization is a way to find the best value of an expensive function you can only test a few times (like tuning a drug dose, where each test costs money and time). When the problem has built-in symmetries (for example, rotating a shape should give the same result), exploiting them can dramatically speed up the search, because symmetry means you learn from one rotation the answer for all rotations — avoiding wasted tests on redundant versions. This paper fixes a long-standing problem: the max kernel, which naturally captures these symmetries, was technically broken for Bayesian Optimization. By repairing it, the paper unlocks efficiency gains on real-world problems.

problem.h2: The symmetry is hidden from the optimizer
paras: Bayesian Optimization searches for the best value of a function by testing smart guesses and learning from the results. A kernel (a way of measuring similarity between two guesses) helps the optimizer understand which untested points are most likely to be good, because similar points tend to have similar values — so if you know one point is good, nearby points are likely good too.

Many real problems have symmetries: rotating a shape doesn't change whether it works well, flipping a circuit layout doesn't change its performance, permuting the order of ingredients in a recipe doesn't matter. A naive optimizer treating these as different points wastes tests — it will re-learn the same lessons for rotated versions instead of pooling what it learned.

The max kernel is a natural way to capture symmetries: instead of comparing two guesses directly, compare the best match of one to any rotated version of the other. But mathematicians discovered that max kernels violate a mathematical property (positive semidefiniteness) that Bayesian Optimization requires. For decades, this has been a barrier: symmetry-aware optimization remained out of reach.

callout.html: The paper makes the max kernel mathematically valid for Bayesian Optimization by projecting it onto the space of positive semidefinite kernels, enabling efficient symmetry-aware optimization.

steps.text: For each pair of guesses, compute how well they align under all possible symmetries.
Pick the best alignment score; this is the max kernel value.
Adjust the max kernel slightly to satisfy the mathematical constraint (positive semidefiniteness).

steps.b: Step 4: Optimizer uses the repaired kernel
steps.text: Bayesian Optimization now knows which untested points are most similar under symmetries.
Because symmetry is exploited, the optimizer finds good answers in fewer evaluations.

paras: The paper changes the kernel (the function that measures similarity between two candidate solutions). Instead of treating each candidate as independent, the kernel now measures similarity under all symmetries of the problem, then applies a mathematical repair to make it valid for Bayesian Optimization.

hidden.name: Maximum cross-orbit similarity under group symmetries
paras: The hidden quantity is the best alignment score when you compare one guess to all rotated or flipped versions of another guess. This alignment score reveals how much information two tests actually share: if they align well under symmetry, learning from one test teaches you about all similar versions, avoiding redundant evaluations.

The paper estimates this by computing the similarity (a kernel value) between one guess and every symmetry-transformed version of another guess, then taking the maximum. The mathematical repair (projection) ensures this max kernel has the right mathematical shape for Bayesian Optimization to use it.

heat.caption: Darker cells: more important. Bright cells show the repair's steps.

reads.html: If two guesses are the same problem rotated, the max kernel gives them high similarity. If they are completely different, similarity is low.

The max kernel compares a guess to all rotated versions of another guess and picks the best match. This raw form violates mathematical rules (positive semidefiniteness), so the paper projects it onto the valid space to keep the symmetry insight while enabling Bayesian Optimization.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: The causal chain
paras: Bayesian Optimization guesses intelligently by building a model of the function from past tests, then proposing the point that looks most promising under that model. To do this correctly, the kernel must capture what makes two guesses similar. A naive kernel doesn't know that a rotated version of a good solution is also good.

The max kernel fixes this: it measures similarity as the best alignment under any symmetry. Two guesses that differ only by a rotation get high similarity, so the optimizer pools their test results — learning faster because redundant tests are avoided. But max kernels were mathematically broken for Bayesian Optimization (not positive semidefinite), which would break the optimizer's probability calculations.

The paper's repair (projection onto positive semidefinite kernels) keeps the max kernel's symmetry-aware insight while fixing the math. The optimizer now correctly uses the extra information: symmetries reduce the effective search space, so fewer tests are needed to converge to the best solution.

stages.s: Past tests: guesses and their scores
Max kernel: measure best match under any symmetry
Build probability model of the function
Fewer tests to convergence, because symmetries pool information

math.words: The projected positive semidefinite max kernel, where for each pair of points x and y, we take the maximum kernel value over all symmetries g of one point, then adjust to ensure positive semidefiniteness.
math.equation: k_proj(x, y) := projection_to_PSD( max_{g in G} k_0(x, g(y)) )
symbols: the set of all symmetries (rotations, flips, etc.)
the guess y transformed by symmetry g
a base kernel measuring raw similarity
the best alignment score across symmetries
the mathematical repair ensuring positive semidefiniteness

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we test two guesses: A (original) and B (rotated 90° version of A).
Base kernel k_0(A, B rotated 0°) = 0.3, k_0(A, B rotated 90°) = 0.95, k_0(A, B rotated 180°) = 0.4, k_0(A, B rotated 270°) = 0.5.
Raw max kernel: max(0.3, 0.95, 0.4, 0.5) = 0.95 — they match well at 90°.
After projection to ensure math validity: k_proj ≈ 0.92 (slightly reduced to fix eigenvalues).
Bayesian Optimization treats A and B as highly similar (0.92) because they are the same problem rotated, so it pools their test results.

math.note: The projection adjusts the max kernel slightly to satisfy mathematical constraints, keeping the symmetry insight while enabling Bayesian Optimization to run correctly.

charts.title: Naive kernel (ignores symmetry)
charts.note: Without symmetry awareness, the optimizer re-learns the same lessons for rotated versions.

charts.title: Projected max kernel
charts.note: The optimizer pools results across rotated versions because high alignment under symmetry means one test teaches it about many variants — learning the answer faster and needing fewer total evaluations.

items.html: If you specify the wrong symmetries (say, claiming a function is rotationally symmetric when it is not), the optimizer will be misled. It will treat different guesses as equivalent when they are not, wasting tests.
For complex symmetry groups, evaluating the max kernel over all symmetries can be slow. If there are thousands of symmetries, computational cost may offset the gain from fewer function evaluations.

items.b: Partial symmetry is hard to exploit.
items.html: Some problems have approximate or conditional symmetries that only hold in part of the search space. Max kernels assume exact, global symmetries. Partial symmetry may not be well captured.
If symmetries are known and efficiently computable, and the function is truly symmetric, the projected max kernel reliably reduces the number of tests needed to find the optimum.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic optimization problem with known rotational or reflective symmetry (for example, finding the maximum of a 2D Gaussian that is radially symmetric). Run Bayesian Optimization three ways: with a naive kernel that ignores symmetry, with the projected max kernel, and with a naive baseline. Plot the best score found vs. the number of tests run. The demo should show that the projected max kernel converges in fewer tests because symmetry is exploited, pooling results across rotations.
demo.closing: The demo makes clear that when symmetries are real and known, the optimizer learns faster by recognizing that rotated or flipped versions of a good solution are also good, without re-testing them.
